data.name: Alone in the Dark: Illumination™
data.detailed_description:
A darkness has fallen over the town of Lorwich. Monstrous hordes emerge from beyond the realm of nightmares to sow chaos on the land. As one of four heroes, you must battle the minions of the old ones with the force of arms, and the power of illumination.

Inspired by the writing of H.P. Lovecraft, Atari’s Alone in the Dark series is recognized as the “Father of the Survival Horror Genre”. Alone in the Dark: Illumination explores this dark legacy in a terrifying action-horror experience.

Battle through dynamic environments filled with bloodthirsty beasts. Build your party as you rescue your companions including the Witch, Engineer and Priest, each with a unique set of special abilities and weapons.

Danger lurks in every shadow. While your friends may help, at the end of the night you are always Alone in the Dark.

  • Four Unique Heroes: The Hunter, the Witch, the Priest and the Engineer each offer unique gameplay experiences with distinctive weapons, skills and powers to unlock.
  • Play as a Team or Alone in the Dark: Play with all four characters in co-operative multiplayer mode, build smaller teams for greater challenge, or face the darkness alone.
  • Diverse Environments: Four campaigns with multiple levels take players through the blasted landscape of Lorwich, and deep below to unearth the mysteries of this forsaken township.
  • Eldritch Horror: Inspired by the writing of H.P. Lovecraft, beings from beyond madness, including Roof Walkers, Shapes and Spawns will haunt your nightmares.
  • Dynamic Environments: Interact with dynamic environmental puzzles to change the structure of the map and advance your quest.
  • Harness the Power of Illumination: Light up maps to create safe zones, and damage your foes.

reviews.review:
[h1]“Winners Don't Use Drugs”
~William S. Sessions, Director, FBI[/h1]

Life is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you're gonna get. OK, OK, that Forrest Gump line is painfully overused, but honestly, it fits the Alone in the Dark series perfectly. Every turn it took was a big surprise. Its creator, Frédérick Raynal, changed the world forever by introducing us to the survival horror genre the way we know it today. Yet... Yeah. It was CAPCOM who ended up being straight with it. While Infogrames with their Alone in the Dark? Well, their story felt a lot like the story of some typical drug addict.

Sure, they made some arguable decisions, but hey! They've got money-money-money!~ 🎵 And at some point, they were on the very top, owning a name that was dear to many – Atari. I mean, Atari, dude! ATARI! That exact Atari that gave many of us our very first gaming memories! And it was all theirs. They even tried to reboot AitD at that point. Some third-party guys already did a solid job with that and pretty much saved the series in their New Nightmare, but no. New Nightmare wasn't cool enough for Infogrames. I mean, they were Atari now! They were the kings of the f*cking world! And being compared to Resident Evil wasn't enough for them. They wanted their stuff to have, like, AAA visuals! And, and, and an open world! And GTA-like cars! Money is one heck of a drug.

As usual with drugs, though (remember, kids, drugs are bad for ya), the effect tends to wear off. And when it does? You find yourself with your face in the gutter. The next thing Infog... I mean, Atari, knew? They were facing bankruptcy. What did they do? Well, they did exactly what pretty much everybody does in such a situation. They panicked. They needed money and they needed it, like, yesterday. So, they dusted off one of the names that they still had a-a-and tried to monetize it the cheapest way possible. What was the cheapest way possible? Well, we all know what it is. They tried to bring things online.

Alone in the Dark Online. I'm not kidding, guys, that's what this game was originally called. Alone in the Dark. ONLINE. Good f*cking grief. What's even weirder, though, is that, while trying to chase trends, they did a really poor job researching the market. Or so it seems. I mean, the original idea here was to turn AitD... into Left 4 Dead. Left 4 Dead, Carl! The game that's even older than that Carl meme I just used! Even though it was only the 2010s, Left 4 Dead's prime was long gone. I mean, people still played it, but it wasn't, like, the trendiest thing you could imagine. Actually, the next big thing was already forming. Damned just came up and, yeah, Dead by Daylight was already on the way. We'll return to those in a bit. For now, it's important to understand that AitD: Illumination (we'll return to the name in a bit too) was... kinda old news long before it came out.

Who did the job, though? Eden Games? I mean, they did a pretty poor job in the 2008 version of Alone in the Dark, can't argue with that, but they made some good games before. But no. At that point, Eden Games was no more. Bankruptcy, remember? Instead, the project was given to... Pure FPS. Now, who THE F*CK is Pure FPS? Well, uh... It was formed by founding members of Plastic Piranha. What, that name means nothing to you either? I really wonder why... I mean, they tried to sell themselves as some sort of “supergroup”, made of people who worked on some really big names, but those were mostly low-level artists, so... Yeah. The real thing behind their back was that online FPS called Rekoil. And yes, there's a very good reason you don't recognize that name either. For Atari, though? It was more than enough. I mean, those were the guys who agreed to work for food AND they already made an online FPS before. HIRED!

If you're a careful reader, though, you've probably noticed one interesting thing. Between Rekoil and AitD: Illumination, there was only one year passing. And if with a small indie team of wannabes and only one year of development in mind you started smelling bull, you're entirely correct. Everything that had a chance to go wrong? Did exactly that in this game. AitD: Illumination doesn't just feel cheap. It doesn't feel like a commercial product at all. If anything, Steam offers lots of much better-polished games for free. But let's return to that later too. Instead, let's start with what this game actually is.

I mean... It LOOKS like they tried to pull a Left 4 Dead. Without having the money or the experience for it. But it looks like they noticed the problem with chasing old trends and switched to a third-person perspective somewhere along the way. They even added a bonus level that offered us pretty much exactly what Dead by Daylight (promised ya I'd return to it) offered. Threw some of dat “go find stuff” into the main game too. What's the main game? Well, it's a co-op-oriented “reach the safe room” kind of thingy (Left 4 Dead, remember?). With enemies being invulnerable without being exposed to light (hence the name, which is one of the things that actually fits the AitD franchise—only the New Nightmare kind of AitD, but still). Sounds cool, right? Well... Not with the game being laughably cheap and clunky, it isn't. Remember, this here is a game that makes Vampire Rain look like a AAA production.

Also, it's buggy as F. There are three zones with four small maps each. With the last map being boss-oriented (like the original AitD, this game tries to be Lovecraftian, so... you're gonna need to prevent Cthulhu from being summoned). But guess what? The key item you're gonna need to do that can spawn in a place where you can't reach it. And you're gonna be, like, out of time. And if you're playing solo (I mean, good luck finding people to play with, lol)? You're gonna barely have enough time to do your thing. Yet you're also gonna fight against bugs. Actually, you know what? Game-breaking bugs are EVERYWHERE. At every single step. Remember me saying they've added some of that Dead by Daylight stuff to the main game? Well, it means you're gonna collect items in order to progress. “Find a certain amount of batteries in order to power up the device”. Sounds easy, right? Well, like I said, there are game-breaking bugs and... Yeah. You know the drill. The game fails to recognize you've already collected all the batteries and keeps saying you need one more. Our “favorite” thing.

The best way to beat the game is to actually play solo while knowing all the workarounds and praying the objectives will update properly (because yes, scripts not working properly is a thing too), but hey! You didn't expect this game to be properly balanced, did you? Because yes, to beat the game solo, you should aim for certain characters and avoid the others. Otherwise, again, you won't have enough time to defeat the boss. Oh, oh! And you can't save. Even in single-player (both single and multiplayer modes use the exact same maps, it's that kind of experience)! And yes, it's almost like they did all that sh*t on purpose. I mean, they probably didn't, yet that's how it feels. Anyway, no save for ya. You run into a bug? Go back to the main menu and replay the whole level. Thankfully, you'll keep your experience (which is also a thing, and characters do level up), but honestly, good gosh...

Anyway, I wrote another lengthy review, but let's be honest, the game doesn't deserve it. It's one of those quick money grabs. Produced in about a year by a small team of wannabes with only one goal in mind – to make some easy money and save Atari from sinking completely. You're not even supposed to play it, really. It's just a thing that... exists. Like, a part of history, you know? If you treat it like one of those “lost alphas” from Hidden Palace? It'll make you sigh and nod understandingly. You attempt to experience AitD: Illumination like a proper product? You're in for one heck of a bad time. Because this candy? It's made by Minny Jackson.
